Beállítom Pontosan öt hónap telt el az áprilisi választás óta, és Magyar Péter ismét országjárásba kezdett, amin Veszprém volt az első állomás. Itt lett képviselő Forsthoffer Ágnes, akivel karöltve a miniszterelnök a színpadra állt szombaton a Megyeház téren, ahova kisebb késéssel érkeztek meg. A miniszterelnök a kampányt felidézve most is emlegette, hogy hát bizony, ő késni szokott. A színpad előtti park már a 16 órás kezdés előtt negyedórával is szinte tele volt. Fotó: Alföldi Dániel István / Telex Forsthoffer Ágnesnek is fontos volt a szeptember 12-i dátum, hiszen éppen egy évvel ezelőtt ezen a napon mutatta be őt a Tisza Párt elnöke a közösség új politikusaként. Az azóta házelnökké lett Forsthoffer a színpadon először szólva meghatottan, de boldogan emlékezett vissza arra a napra. Ezután rátért, hogy miért tartja fontosnak, hogy most ismét az emberekkel legyenek: mert szerinte veszélyes, ha a politikusok eltávolodnak az emberektől. „Talán az elmúlt időszak legnagyobb eredménye nem is egy-egy elfogadott törvény, parlamenti döntés. Hanem az, hogy a magyar emberek hangja szabad és hallatszik.” – mondta Forsthoffer, és a térségből is mondott példát erre. Szerinte a Balaton mellett élők egyre hangosabban kimondják, hogy elég volt a part beépítéséből, és hogy a helyiek helyett a befektetők és a kiváltságosok érdeke az első. „Ez a hang is célba fog érni” – mondta a balatonfüredi körzet országgyűlési képviselője. Szerinte az, hogy a közösségek hallatják a hangjukat, fontos része a politikának, mivel a demokrácia nemcsak a négyévenkénti szavazásból áll. Fotó: Alföldi Dániel István / Telex A gyűlés előtt egy nyugdíjas férfi egyedül állt a színpad közelében, mint elmondta, azért, hogy közelről láthassa, megváltozott-e Magyar Péter április óta. Amikor a Tisza Párt elnöke a választás előtt országjárásán először fordult meg Veszprémben, az idős férfi akkor is közel állt a színpadhoz. A miniszterelnök fellépésén ő ugyanazt a határozottságot és őszinteséget látja, mint korábban, ezért benne nincs csalódottság, bár a saját korosztályában még most is lát elégedetlenséget a választási eredmény miatt. A tömegben hallgatta Magyar Pétert egy fiatal házaspár is, akik már nagyon kíváncsiak voltak arra, mit fog elmondani a miniszterelnök egy olyan országjáráson, amelyet már nem a kampánya alatt tart. A férfi azt mondta, lassan őrölnek a kerekek a politikában, nem sok ideje kormányoz Magyar, és tudja, hogy ez nem elég 16 év bűneinek helyrehozására. Ugyanakkor vannak, akik már kezdenek elégedetlenkedni, a pár női tagja szerint a gyermekvédelem és a korrupció kezelése olyan ügyek, amikben már eredményekre van szükség. „Nekem ez hiányzott” – mondta Magyar Péter arról, hogy az országjárás továbbra is közel áll hozzá. Sokan mondják neki mostanában, hogy milyen fáradtnak tűnik, és hogy menjen pihenni, mondta a miniszterelnök, aki szerint Ruff Bálint Miniszterelnökséget vezető miniszter is folyton ezzel jön. Magyar azt mondta: „Én nem úgy pihenek és nem úgy tudok feltöltődni, hogy lefekszem otthon és olvasgatok, bár lehet, hogy régen volt ilyen, erről már leszoktam. Én így érzem jól magam.” Fotó: Alföldi Dániel István / Telex Magyar arról is beszélt, hogy a Tisza Szigetek újra aktivizálták magukat, és várakozásai szerint szeptember végére meglesz a közösségek országos koordinátora is. Ezt a személyt most választják majd ki abból a nagyjából ezerből, aki jelentkezett erre a feladatra. A szigetek munkája folytatódik, és Magyar Péter szerint az a lendület sem ért véget, amivel pártja választást tudott nyerni tavasszal. „Látom, hogy a propagandisták már fáradnak, már el sem jöttek ide” – mondta a Fideszhez közeli sajtót felemlegetve, amivel ugyancsak a választási kampány reflexeit idézte. Szerinte most kiderült, hogy az egykori kormánypárt mellett álló újságírókat eddig nem a hazaszeretet vezérelte, mivel ha nincs közpénz, akkor már nem folytatják, amit eddig csináltak. „Hova tovább?” Ezzel a kérdéssel kanyarodott rá Magyar Péter arra, hogy 123 nap kormányzással a háta mögött jelenleg mit tud kínálni az embereknek. „Biztosan nem tetszik mindenkinek az, amit teszünk” – mondta, elismerve, hogy nem is tudna mindenkinek megfelelni, de ő akkor is minden magyar miniszterelnöke szeretne lenni. Szerinte kormányát a hazaszeretet és a lelkesedés vezeti, még ha néha túl is megy a lelkesedés – mondta a kormányfő, aki most jóval derűsebb hangulatban beszélt, mint ahogyan a parlamenti üléseken szokott. „123 napja kormányzunk és néha úgy érzem mintha az egész elmúlt 16 évet rajtunk kérnék számon” – mondta Magyar, aki azért szóba hozta elődje, Orbán Viktor felelősségét is. Tőle nem vár semmit, ahogy azt sem várta, hogy megoldja helyette a paksi helyzetet az energiaválság napjaiban. Arra azonban számított volna a korábbi kormányfőtől, hogy megjelenik az egyeztetésen, és beszámol az elmúlt évek Paksot érintő mulasztásairól és döntéseiről. Többször említette a 123 napot, és azt, hogy a program, amelynek a teljesítését vállalták, négy évre vonatkozik. Ezért megértést is kért, hiszen a kormány nem tud mindent egyszerre teljesíteni, és csak lépésről-lépésre tudnak haladni. Ha átadják a kormányzást négy év múlva, akár valaki másnak is, akkor büszke szeretne majd lenni az elért eredményekre. Tudja, hogy a mézes hetek, habár sokáig kitartanak, nem maradnak örökre. Hallja a kritikákat is, és mindenkit biztosított arról, hogy ha valamit jogosnak tartanak, akkor azon változtatni is fognak. Hiszen nem azért hagytak fel a politikusok a korábbi életüket, hogy olyanok legyenek, mint a korábbi kormány, mondta. Fotó: Alföldi Dániel István / Telex A miniszterelnök két miniszterét is nevesítette, és arra kérte közönségét, hogy tapsolják meg a kormánytagok munkáját. Az első Kármán András volt, akinek szerinte hatalmas érdemei vannak abban, hogy a kormány megalakulása után stabilizálni tudták az ország pénzügyi helyzetét. Ha ez nem sikerül, az ország könnyen fizetésképtelenné is válhatott volna, mondta Magyar. Vitézy Dávidot is említette név szerint, mint aki közlekedési miniszterként kulcsszerepet játszott az európai uniós források megszerzésében. A legnagyobb tapsot érezhetően Vitézy kapta a hallgatóságtól, de Gyurkó Szilvia államtitkár említésére is lelkesen reagáltak – ő éppen a délelőtt mutatta be Magyar Péterrel közösen azt a nagy gyermekvédelmi jelentést , amit Kátai-Németh Vilmos szociális és családügyi miniszterrel közösen készítettek. A nagyjából másfél órás beszéde után magyar azzal köszönt el veszprémi hallgatóságától, hogy szeretne az emberek szemébe nézni, és úgy folytatni országjárást, amelyről már meg sem tudta mondani, hogy hányadik ilyen útja pontosan. Tervei szerint így is heti 2–3 települést akar végigjárni a következő időszakban. Beszéde végeztével a színpadra hívta Veszprém megye összes országgyűlési képviselőjét, akik egymás vállát átkarolva fel is vonultak, majd azt kérte, a közönséggel együtt énekeljék el a Tavaszi szelet „a régi idők emlékére.” Kedvenceink Partnereinktől Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.text: Goldsmiths students made their feelings known in Deptford, south-east London, on Friday. Photograph: Lily Renshaw/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Goldsmiths students made their feelings known in Deptford, south-east London, on Friday. Photograph: Lily Renshaw/The Guardian Goldsmiths, University of London Goldsmiths fine art students call for compensation over record tutor strike With industrial action over job cuts heading into its 21st week, students at famed London college are unhappy Richard Adams Education editor Mon 26 Oct 2026 05.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Students arriving at Goldsmiths, University of London this autumn found a campus embroiled in a bitter industrial dispute that has upended timetables and disrupted courses. “I was really excited to start my studies at Goldsmiths,” one international student told the Guardian at a gathering of unhappy students on Friday. “But when I first arrived, I was quite shocked because almost all the induction sessions seemed to turn into discussions about strikes.” The international student was one of the unlucky ones, having enrolled on the master of fine art (MFA) course that has been among the worst affected, with 10 out of the 12 usual tutors on strike, and students now saying they want compensation from the university for their lost learning. Edinburgh joins UK universities heading for strikes as cuts spread through entire sector Read more Florence Sweeney, a part-time student, said there had been “virtually no teaching” so far this term for many of the fine arts students, and that a group were seeking remuneration. “Not only has it been a financial drain, but I can see my cohort are very distressed and anxious, and some are depressed by what’s going on,” Sweeney said. “Some people have moved from the other side of the world, and for them it’s such a risk. To not even get welcomed or proper briefings, it’s really disappointing, especially for a place with such a good reputation for producing exceptional contemporary artists.” Goldsmiths is famous for the stellar array of artists among its former students, including Steve McQueen , Sarah Lucas and Damien Hirst . But it has been financially squeezed in recent years by falling applications in its core humanities subjects and the erosion of domestic tuition fees, setting off what one staff member described as “non-stop” rounds of redundancies and restructuring. Now entering its 21st week and with no end in sight, the current strike involving University and College Union (UCU) staff is the longest in living memory in British higher education, originating from a staff marking boycott in April over proposed job cuts. Goldsmiths’ management responded firmly to the boycott by deducting 100% of pay from those involved. The union argued that amounted to a lockout and a formal ballot followed, so that since early June a group of UCU members at the south-east London university have been on indefinite strike. Joe Newman, a Goldsmiths UCU branch co-president, said: “We’ve resisted as much as we can over the last two rounds of restructuring and redundancies. But right now, the scale of the action that we are taking is in response to the unprecedented scale and speed of the cuts management are pursuing.” The Goldsmiths crisis: how cuts and culture wars sent universities into a death spiral Read more Newman said students were largely supportive because they “have more in common with staff on precarious contracts than with senior managers on six-figure salaries”, who he said wanted more savings despite earlier cuts. “When we talk to the students about why we are on strike, of course there are a range of opinions, but overwhelmingly they are just aghast,” Newman said. “The students who have been here longer have seen the impact of previous cuts and seen how things have only got worse. Students who are new can’t believe that management is about to launch an incredibly messy redundancy process.” The university said only “a small portion of our staff – around 8.5%” were on strike, leaving most students unaffected, and that it had offered significant compromises to the union, including a pause on compulsory redundancies. But it was not prepared to scrap the 100% pay deductions for the marking boycott, saying it had spent significant amounts to ease the impact on students. “Like many UK higher education institutions, Goldsmiths faces significant financial challenges, which need to be addressed to ensure its future sustainability,” a spokesperson for the university said. “We recognise colleagues’ right to take industrial action, but continued disruption risks further impacting students’ education and the university’s hard-earned reputation as a world-renowned academic institution in the long-term. “We are doing everything we can to monitor and mitigate disruption, and are supporting students on courses affected by this strike action, including offering students’ regular updates, meetings with their schools and other appropriate support as needed.” UK universities face ‘financial crisis’ amid collapse in international students Read more MFA students said they had been disappointed by the impact on the two-year course, which charges nearly £15,000 a year for full-time UK students and £33,000 for international students. John Carver, a part-time student in his second year, said he had decided to suspend his studies after attending a “dismal” departmental meeting at the start of term. “I’m a mature student, time matters to me, and I would be going into a chaotic situation where tutors have been on strike for so long. There wasn’t any light at the end of the tunnel,” Carver said. “The tutors at Goldsmiths are fantastic, and the way they interact in tutorials, when you do get them, it’s as good as it gets, you build relationships with all the tutors. But what’s going on now is that [replacement] tutors are being brought in who don’t know the students and it’s not as impressive, to put it politely.” James Evans, an international student from the US, said visa and funding restrictions meant he had to stick with the MFA course despite the disruption. “Towards the end of last year, in the first days of the strike, I never received marks back, the end-of-term show wasn’t graded. The marks aren’t the important part, but the dialogue is, and there were very important fixtures for the year that went without any discussion. It was a bit frustrating. But this year it’s been worse,” Evans said. “Our fees went up this year, [and] as an international student they were exorbitant to begin with. There’s still no feedback on projects from last year, but beyond that there’s no structure, barely any communication. We’ve been left to our own devices. It’s been difficult to navigate.” Explore more on these topics Goldsmiths, University of London Students Higher education Universities University funding International students Student experience news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Education Schools Teachers Universities Students

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Heavy machinery and emergency personnel work on Wednesday at the scene of a collision between two high-speed trains in the village of Urda, Toledo, Spain. Photograph: Óscar del Pozo/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Heavy machinery and emergency personnel work on Wednesday at the scene of a collision between two high-speed trains in the village of Urda, Toledo, Spain. Photograph: Óscar del Pozo/AFP/Getty Images Spain Spain begins mourning period after train crash as search continues for victims in wreckage Emergency services, drones and dog unit continue to comb carriages as Civil Guard sets up clinics for relatives to provide DNA samples Sam Jones and Ashifa Kassam in Madrid Thu 29 Oct 2026 07.11 EDT First published on Thu 29 Oct 2026 01.31 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Spain has begun three days of mourning to commemorate the 69 people who died in a high-speed rail collision as hospitals continue to treat dozens of injured passengers and relatives wait for news of their loved ones. The trains – one from Spain’s state-owned Renfe and the other from the private rail company Iryo – were heading from Madrid on Wednesday to the southern region of Andalucía on the same line when they collided just before 9am. After the Iryo train came to a halt, the other slammed into its rear, knocking several carriages off the track near the town of Urda in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha. Officials said on Wednesday another 107 people had needed medical treatment in hospital, including 15 who were in a serious condition. The deadly crash came 10 months after 46 people were killed and dozens more injured after two trains – again, one from Renfe and one from Iryo – collided on the same line near the town of Adamuz in Andalucía. The disaster has raised fresh questions about safety on Spain’s large, modern high-speed rail network after the transport minister, Óscar Puente, said rear-end collisions such as Wednesday’s were “highly unlikely”, and suggested the accident could have been caused by human error under “inexplicable” circumstances. View image in fullscreen Officials work at the scene of the train crash. Photograph: Pablo Blázquez Domínguez/Getty Images He said the LZB signalling system, which automatically halts a train if the line ahead is occupied, had gone down at about 8.30am local time owing to a computer malfunction. As a result, an estimated six trains had been halted along a stretch of about 63km of track, Puente added. The task of monitoring the rail lines then fell to a 24-hour command centre in Madrid. Minutes after the computer malfunction, the centre instructed at least two of the trains to continue as normal, despite the fact that there was still a “stop signal” in place, the minister added. “It was the control centre, through its operators, that made the decision to resume traffic, under circumstances that, from our point of view, are inexplicable,” he said. “Clearly, it was a wrong decision.” Emergency services combed through the wreckage through the night to find more victims, hoisting pieces of mangled metal with cranes. At daybreak, police once again launched drones to survey the crash site. One more body was found overnight, bringing the death toll to 69. View image in fullscreen World Central Kitchen delivers meals to emergency services and security forces at the scene of a collision between two high-speed trains. Photograph: Angeles Visdomine/EPA Emiliano García-Page, the leader of the Castilla-La Mancha regional government, said on Thursday morning that rescue teams did not think they would find any more bodies in one damaged carriage that was ‌still overturned, but added that body parts had been found that would need to be identified. “Yesterday we experienced a catastrophe that without a doubt has left all of Spain in shock,” said García-Page. He confirmed that 50 of the 110 people who had been taken to hospitals in the region were still being treated. The prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, speaking during a visit to the emergency command centre in the city of Toledo, said the authorities were doing all they could to establish the cause of the crash and prevent another rail tragedy. “I’d like to let all Spaniards know that every institution that is part of the state – from the smallest municipality to the government of Spain – is working day and night, not only to provide a response to the families of the victims, but also, of course, to uncover every last detail of this tragedy and to strengthen safety measures so that something like this never happens again.” Meanwhile, train drivers in Spain went ahead with a previously planned strike to press for more investment in railway safety after what was Europe’s deadliest train accident since a 2013 derailment in Santiago de Compostela in north-west Spain that killed 80 people. ‘It all happened in a split-second’: survivors recount details of deadly train crash in Spain Read more The Guardia Civil police force has set up four offices in the cities of Madrid, Toledo, Córdoba and Seville to enable relatives to provide DNA samples and help identify victims. Blood donation points have also been set up in Castilla-La Mancha and Madrid. The force said 64 people had been reported missing by relatives by Thursday morning. A school in Urda, which lies about 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid, has been turned into an information centre where relatives can inquire about loved ones. Teams of Red Cross workers offered support to groups of people who had arrived, some of them in tears. Carmen García, a Red Cross psychologist, said “long and hard hours” lay ahead and that “every person will manage it in their own way”. She added: “We have people who are in shock, who haven’t taken onboard what has happened, angry people, sad, worried people. The grieving will be complicated.” 1:31 Spain in mourning after fatal rail crash, says Spanish prime minister - video José Miguel Fernández, a parish priest in Urda, joined the emergency services in offering support to the victims’ families. “It is important for relatives to find their loved ones, even if they have died, because the grieving process is quicker when you have been able to say goodbye at that final moment,” he told Onda Cero radio. Second fatal train collision this year casts doubt over Spain’s high-speed rail network Read more Survivors have spoken of being thrown from their seats by the impact of the crash, and of trying to help the injured in the immediate aftermath. The first victim to be named included a 31-year-old Guardia civil officer, José Manuel Chacón. The national law enforcement agency expressed its “deepest condolences” to his family, friends and colleagues. Spanish media said the missing included a former minister for the conservative People’s party (PP) and several foreigners, who were thought to be on holiday in Spain. The PP leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, called for an immediate investigation into what had happened, as well as a “complete and independent review” of Spain’s entire rail network. “Spain has the right to know what is going on with its infrastructure,” he told reporters.
